title: Diagnosing and Recovering from Observation-Space Shift at Long-Horizon Skill Seams

paper.title: Diagnosing and Recovering from Observation-Space Shift at Long-Horizon Skill Seams
paper.abstract:
Abstract Long-horizon robotic manipulation is often built by chaining skills that are trained independently.
Although individual skills can be reliable in isolation, long-horizon task performance can degrade sharply when these skills are chained: each downstream skill must start from the state produced by its predecessor rather than from its training distribution.
We study this failure mode, known as Observation-Space Shift (OSS), and investigate what aspects are responsible for such skill-seam failures.
Through privileged simulator resets, we identify that the dominant shift arises from displaced scene state (e.g., an open drawer or secondary objects left behind by preceding skills), rather than from the robot joint configuration or the object manipulated by the downstream skill.
To test this diagnosis, we build a fully learned detect–restore–resume system that restores the components the analysis identifies: a task-progress monitor detects the stall, a learned policy restores those components, and seam-robust fine-tuning lets the skill resume .
It recovers the seam where every tested alternative fails, which is evidence for the diagnosis rather than a general purpose method.
On the BOSS-44 benchmark, our system improves full-chain success from 7.6% to 26.5%, a 3.5 × 3.5\times improvement over the base policy and 51% of a privileged restoration oracle.
In contrast, best-of- K K resampling, a Diffusion Policy, and world-model-based baselines fail to recover from the evaluated OSS seam states.
During real-robot experiments on a real Franka arm running π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy, the same progress monitor is limited by external camera observability, yet closing the loop still recovers some otherwise-terminal failures. This motivates wrist and gripper sensing.
These results suggest that some long-horizon composition failures are better addressed by restoring the scene before resuming the policy, rather than retrying from an off-support state.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Long-horizon robotic manipulation often requires composing multiple skills into a single task [ 1 , 2 ] . For example, a robot may first open a drawer, then move an object, and finally place it at a target location. A common strategy is to train individual manipulation skills independently and execute them sequentially in a chain at deployment. Although these skills can be reliable when evaluated from their own training distributions, long-horizon task performance can degrade drastically once they are chained together. The challenge arises at the skill seams , where one skill terminates and the next begins: A downstream skill does not start from the canonical initial states on which it was trained; instead, it inherits whatever scene state its predecessor leaves behind. For example, an “open drawer” skill may leave the drawer open before a “place bowl” skill, trained with the drawer closed, begins execution. The downstream skill is therefore asked to act from an unfamiliar state and may stall even though it succeeds reliably in isolation. This mismatch between the downstream skill’s training distribution and the state encountered during skill composition is known as Observation-Space Shift (OSS) [ 2 ] . On the three-skill chains studied in BOSS-44 [ 2 ] , success through the chain drops from 88.5 % 88.5\% after executing the first skill, to 34.3 % 34.3\% after two skills (one seam), and to 7.6 % 7.6\% after all three skills (two seams), despite the component skills achieving 79.0 % 79.0\% average success when evaluated independently from their canonical initial states. Fig. 1: Detect, restore, resume at a skill seam. A chained skill collapses when it starts from the previous skill’s off-support terminal state; a task-progress monitor detects the stall, a learned restoration skill returns the displaced scene to support, and the chain resumes. What changes at a skill seam that causes the downstream skill to fail? We consider three potential sources of shift: the preceding skill may (1) leave the robot arm in an unfamiliar state; (2) displace the object manipulated by the downstream skill; or (3) alter other elements of the scene. To identify which components are responsible, we diagnose OSS through privileged simulator interventions. Using a teleportation oracle and component-wise resets, we selectively restore different state components to their canonical values. We find that (1) resetting the robot arm provides little improvement; (2) the object manipulated by the downstream skill is typically already close to its canonical position; and (3) the dominant recovery comes from restoring articulated scene state (e.g., an open drawer) and secondary objects (i.e., other objects displaced by preceding skills but not manipulated by the downstream skill). Moreover, these effects are complementary: restoring articulation or secondary objects individually yields only partial gains, whereas restoring them jointly recovers substantially more of the oracle performance. This diagnosis suggests that recovery should modify the state responsible for the failure rather than repeatedly invoke the policy from off-support states. As shown in Fig. 1 , we introduce a detect–restore–resume framework: a fully learned, non-privileged system that recovers much of the oracle from cameras and proprioception alone. A task-progress monitor detects when execution has stalled. A learned restoration policy modifies the displaced scene state, after which the downstream skill resumes execution. Since learned restoration only approximately returns the scene to its canonical state, we additionally apply seam-robust prevention fine-tuning on post-restoration hand-off states to improve robustness during re-entry. On BOSS-44, our system improves three-skill full-chain success from 7.6 % 7.6\% to 26.5 % 26.5\% , compared with 51.8 % 51.8\% under a privileged oracle that exactly restores the scene to its canonical state. A matched re-home-and-retry baseline reaches only 12.9 % 12.9\% , showing that the improvement cannot be explained simply by additional execution attempts. Best-of- K K resampling and a Diffusion Policy trained on the same canonical demonstrations also fail from the evaluated OSS seam states, indicating that retrying or changing the policy architecture alone does not resolve these failures. On a real Franka arm with a π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy, the same monitor runs unchanged but transfers only weakly from an exterior camera. Closing the loop also recovers some otherwise-terminal failures, a proof of concept that isolates the observability (wrist and gripper sensing) as an important requirement for deployment. Our contributions are three-fold. • We provide a diagnosis of OSS at long-horizon skill seams. Through privileged simulator interventions, we show that skill-seam failures are driven primarily by displaced articulation and secondary scene objects. • We propose a learned detect–restore–resume framework for long-horizon skill composition. The system detects stalled execution, restores the displaced scene toward the downstream support, and resumes execution using only deployable observations at test time. • Experiments on both BOSS-44 demonstrate that our framework achieves a 3.5 × 3.5\times improvement in full-chain success, outperforming other baselines. We provide empirical analysis of when restoration is a better intervention than retry. On a real Franka, the same monitor runs unchanged but it limited by exterior-camera observability. Closing the loop recovers a fraction of otherwise-terminal failures, a proof of concept that motivates wrist and gripper sensing.

sections.heading: II Related Work
sections.text: Skill chaining, observation-space shift, and recovery. Composing pretrained skills into long-horizon behavior is central to hierarchical and library-based control [ 3 , 4 , 2 , 1 ] , where a transition succeeds only when one skill’s termination region meets the next’s initiation set [ 5 , 6 ] . A seam is a violation of that condition. The mechanism is the behavior-cloning covariate shift at composition, where a downstream skill inherits a state its predecessor produced but never trained on [ 7 , 8 ] . This is not specific to small policies: generalist vision-language-action models [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] and modern imitation learners [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] clone actions and inherit the same off-support behavior when chained. Unlike work that reports chaining loss as an aggregate drop, we localize the shift causally to specific state components. Prior fixes act at training time, regularizing a skill’s terminal distribution toward the next initiation set [ 17 ] or appending recovery and correction data [ 18 ] . Test-time recovery instead retrieves and replays demonstration sub-trajectories [ 19 ] , backtracks to a prior skill, takes object-centric keypoint steps back onto the manifold [ 20 ] , or learns local RL recovery policies [ 21 ] . We test faithful instances of retrieval, backtracking, and library-inverse correction and find none re-manipulates the displaced scene. Our restoration skill supplies that behavior as a learned reset controller, the objective of reset-free RL and learned resets [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] , but invoked at a detected seam rather than every episode. It is trained with SAC [ 25 ] and RLPD [ 26 ] from real failure states and distilled to a camera-only student. We compare it against a training-time prevention condition built with data generation [ 27 ] rather than only asserting the distinction. Detection and test-time alternatives. Detecting task failure without labels has converged on task-progress and value estimation from pixels: Generative Value Learning [ 28 ] elicits per-frame completion from a VLM, and process-reward models such as Robometer [ 29 ] train per-frame progress on robot data. Our monitor keeps the progress-as-normalized-time target but trains a ∼ 1 \sim\!1 M-parameter head over a frozen encoder with an added success/stall contrast loss, and fires a calibrated stagnation trigger in the spirit of distribution-free failure detection [ 30 , 31 ] . Unlike runtime monitors that add temporal-consistency terms [ 32 ] or world-model prediction surprise, we find progress alone is the correctly signed signal at stalls. The alternative to restoration is planning or search: imagine-score-execute pipelines plan with learned dynamics [ 33 , 34 , 35 , 36 ] and sampling-based shooting (e.g., MPPI [ 37 ] ) selects actions by simulated return, while a separate line scales test-time compute by sampling K K rollouts and keeping the best [ 38 ] . Evaluated from OSS seams, a world model as generator, monitor, or planner gives no benefit or is falsified, and best-of- K K cannot select what the policy cannot produce. These both point to restoration over planning or sampling.

sections.heading: III Problem Formulation
sections.text: Setting. We study three-skill chains on BOSS-44, a benchmark of 44 44 kitchen and living-room manipulation tasks drawn from LIBERO-90 [ 1 ] . Tasks are simulated in robosuite [ 39 ] on the MuJoCo physics engine [ 40 ] , with a 7 7 -DOF Panda under 20 20 Hz OSC delta control. A chain ch3 ​ _ ​ N \mathrm{ch3}\_N is an ordered triple of BOSS-44 tasks run in one continuous episode. For example, ch3 ​ _ ​ 2 \mathrm{ch3}\_2 is open the drawer → \to place the bowl on the plate → \to place the bowl in the cabinet . All ten catastrophic chains are reorderings of the shared 13 13 -skill set. When skill i i ’s goal is satisfied, the environment advances to skill i + 1 i{+}1 , re-homing only the arm (joint and velocity state) while objects and articulation carry over. That carry-over is what we study. A three-skill chain is the shortest that contains two seams, so a downstream skill can inherit shift that has already compounded across an upstream one. It is the minimal setting in which seam collapse is more than a single-transition artifact, and we adopt it throughout. Each skill is a per-task BC-Transformer policy (one checkpoint per task, frozen throughout) reading a fixed exterior camera (“agentview”), wrist RGB, and 16 16 -D proprioception (arm joint and gripper state). We report chain success at three depths: L 0 L_{0} (first skill only), L 1 L_{1} (through the first seam, two skills), and L 2 L_{2} (all three skills, the full chain and our primary metric). Observation-Space Shift. Observation-Space Shift (OSS) is the covariate shift a chained skill faces at a seam [ 2 ] . Let 𝒟 i \mathcal{D}_{i} be the canonical initial-state distribution skill i i was trained from. In a chain, skill i i is executed from s ∼ T i − 1 s\sim T_{i-1} , the terminal-state distribution of its predecessor. Seam collapse is the failure that occurs because T i − 1 T_{i-1} is a covariate shift off 𝒟 i \mathcal{D}_{i} ’s support, and BC provides no off-support correction. We make this quantitative below. Scope of restoration. In TAMP terms, the effects of skill i − 1 i{-}1 split into preconditions of skill i i and side effects unrelated to it. Recovery by restoration is well defined only for side effects, and only when the change is reversible toward a known canonical target. The inherited change is itself a precondition, like opening a drawer before placing an object in it, and restoring it destroys what the next skill needs. Sec. V-D maps this boundary empirically. Benchmark subset and evaluation. We evaluate 20 20 episodes per chain, and extend each estimate to five disjoint seeds by sliding the init-state window. Our primary analyses focus on the 10 10 catastrophic chains (base-policy L 2 L_{2} ≤ 0.30 \,\leq 0.30 ), which exercise 13 13 of the 44 44 skills across three LIBERO-90 kitchen scenes whose seams leaves a drawer open S1 (top/bottom drawers, a black bowl, a plate), S2 (top drawer, black bowls, a plate), S4 (bottom drawer, a wine bottle and bowl, where the object grasp is the hardest). Seam collapse is most severe. The collapse is noticeably seen on some chains where chain success falls 0.885 → 0.343 → 0.076 0.885\to 0.343\to 0.076 across the two seams, with each skill individually competent: evaluated from their own canonical initial states the frozen skills succeed at 0.79 0.79 on average (Table I ), so the collapse is composition, not skill incompetence. Across the full benchmark, OSS induces a mean Ratio Performance Delta (RPD, the relative success drop) of 0.45 0.45 over one seam and 0.51 0.51 over two [ 2 ] ; the catastrophic chains are the severe tail of that distribution. sections.heading: IV Method: Detect, Restore, Resume
sections.text: Recovering a chained skill requires noticing it was stalled, putting the scene back on-support, and letting the skill tolerate an imperfect hand-back. We add one learned component for each, detect , restore , and resume , leaving the base skills frozen. All three read only deployable inputs (RGB cameras and proprioception; Fig. 1 ).

sections.heading: IV-A Detect: a task-progress monitor with a calibrated trigger
sections.text: Detect answers one question: has the current skill stopped making progress? A task-progress head scores each frame’s position within a skill, and the trigger fires when that score stops rising (Fig. 3 ). Prediction-surprise signals fail here: at seams the robot stalls, so the next frame is nearly identical and trivially predictable, and surprise becomes anti-predictive ((Sec. V-B )). A stalled robot cannot manufacture progress, so the progress signal stays correctly signed. Trigger. The alarm is progress-slope stagnation over an 8 8 -sample window (not absolute level, which is low early in every skill), fired when the statistic exceeds a threshold τ \tau for 3 3 consecutive samples. τ \tau is set by split-conformal calibration on success demos [ 30 ] . Since seam states are off-support its formal guarantee need not hold, so we fix the operating point empirically on cached rollouts ( 0.95 0.95 true-positive, 7 % 7\% false-alarm; Sec. V-E ).

sections.heading: IV-B Restore: a learned scene-restoration skill
sections.text: Restoration must return the components the diagnosis singles out, like the displaced articulation and the secondary objects prior skills leave behind (Sec. V-A ), to where the next skill is competent. No existing action source does this, and four candidates (a scripted controller, demonstration replay, backtracking, and a library inverse skill) all fail since skill libraries encode task progress, not scene restoration (Sec. V-B ). We therefore learn the behavior with RL under a dense reward. Integration. At an alarm the restoration actor runs closed-loop until the drawer returns to canonical ( ∑ | Δ artic | < 0.02 \sum|\Delta_{\text{artic}}|<0.02 ) or a 150 150 -step cap fires. The arm then re-homes and the skill resumes with a cleared observation history. Up to r max = 2 r_{\max}{=}2 alarms are handled per skill. Deployability. The state-based teacher is distilled to a camera-only student (dual RGB and 16 16 -D proprioception; 0.85 / 0.90 0.85/0.90 vs. teacher, Fig. 4b ), so the loop uses zero simulator state. The same controller runs unchanged in simulation and on hardware behind a minimal robot API (reset, step, observe, home).

sections.heading: IV-C Resume: seam-robust prevention fine-tuning
sections.text: Resume makes the downstream skill tolerate an imperfect hand-back, since restoration returns the scene only approximately to support. We fine-tune each post-seam skill on the deep hand-off states the recovery loop reaches, which raw rollouts almost never produce. On its own this is marginal, adding to recovery only at a trend level (Sec. V-C ); we treat it as complementary to restoration.

sections.heading: IV-D Implementation Details
sections.text: Detector Architecture. A frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/16 [ 41 ] encodes a 128 × 128 128{\times}128 frame to a patch-token grid. A small task-conditioned head (a FiLM-conditioned [ 42 ] ResNet, ∼ 1 \sim\!1 M parameters) regresses the progress logit. The head is trained with three self-supervised losses on strong-policy rollouts: an absolute-progress anchor (BCE to t / ( T − 1 ) t/(T{-}1) , GVL-style [ 28 ] ), an intra-demo ranking loss (later frames score higher), and a success/stall contrast that pushes frames from failed-window tails below success frames, the only failure-specific signal available without labels. All numbers are cross-validated by chain (each chain scored by the fold that never trained on it). Restoration Reset library. Every monitor alarm records the full simulator state, and each recorded failure state is paired with its exact restoration target (the canonical articulation and object values the oracle would teleport to). This yields per-scene libraries of realistic failure states ( ∼ 5.7 \sim\!5.7 k / 4.6 /4.6 k / 3.6 /3.6 k for S1/S2/S4, ∼ 14 \sim\!14 k total) with dense, automatic targets: no reward engineering, no labels, and every rollout starts in a state that occurs mid-chain. Restoration Agent. A render-free, state-based teacher is trained per scene by SAC [ 25 ] (drawer S1/S2) and demonstration-augmented RLPD [ 26 ] (drawer S4, where SAC’s grasp exploration stalls). The reward is the distance of the displaced component to its known target, with a disturbance penalty on non-target objects and a success bonus. Episodes are short ( ≤ 150 \leq\!150 steps) and success-terminated. State-based training needs no rendering, so it parallelizes on CPU. Drawer restoration reaches 1.00 / 0.93 / 0.78 1.00/0.93/0.78 (S1/S2/S4) at the skill level (Fig. 4a ). Prevention fine-tuning. We fine-tune each post-seam skill on 581 581 deep hand-off demonstrations collected through the recovery loop, mixed with the original per-skill demonstrations. We keep the checkpoint that minimizes seam-window loss subject to a forgetting constraint on the base-policy validation loss. Scaling this set 10 × 10\times (to 6073 6073 ) does not improve it (Sec. VII ).

Detection is scored by the AUROC of the alarm statistic over per-seam windows. Overview. We structure the evaluation by first localizing what causes seam collapse and must be restored (Sec. V-A ). We then show that no simpler alternative, like test-time compute, a stronger base policy, or a world model, recovers it (Sec. V-B ). We then present the deployed detect–restore–resume system and its recovery (Sec. V-C ). Finally, we analyze when restoration is the right action, and why (Sec. V-D ). We also quantify detector quality and deployability (Sec. V-E ) and test transfer to a real robot (Sec. V-F ).

sections.heading: V-D When restoration is the right fix
sections.text: The diagnosis says what to restore, but here we ask when the deployed restoration actually helps, isolating the recovery action per chain (matched re-home + + retry vs. learned restoration, no prevention; Tab. V ). The outcome tracks one variable: our restorer acts only on the drawer , so what matters is whether the seam’s blocking displacement is a drawer that the downstream skill does not itself operate. (i) An off-canonical drawer blocks a non-drawer skill (a bowl onto the cabinet top while a drawer is stuck open, ch3_2,3 ): restoration clears the obstruction and is decisive ( → 0.28 0\!\to\!0.28 ), where a retry cannot move the drawer. (ii) The downstream skill is a drawer operation ( ch3_16,8,12 ): restoring the drawer undoes the skill’s own effect, so a retry is better and restoration can regress an already-working chain ( → 0.21 0.32\!\to\!0.21 ). (iii) The blocker is a displaced free object ( ch3_15,17,20 ): the drawer restorer has no matching action and the chain is unrecovered. The finding is that restoration helps exactly when a restorable component blocks a skill that does not operate it. We tested the prescribed fix directly: a learned object restorer reaches 0.65 0.65 at the skill level in isolation but only L 2 L_{2} ≈ 0.10 \,{\approx}\,0.10 at the chain level (vs. 0.265 0.265 for drawer restoration), so object-blocked seams remain open.

sections.text: The simulation monitor runs unchanged on hardware, but its limit there is observability. We ran the loop on a Franka arm driven by a served, LoRA-fine-tuned π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 43 ] vision-language-action policy over three object-rearrangement chains (nine skills spanning shared-object, picking, and placing seams), 15 15 trials per chain, with place-only restoration under a matched step budget (both conditions get 200 200 steps per skill, with restoration counted inside it). The hardware restoration is a language-prompted π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} behavior, not the distilled camera-only student of Sec. IV-B . The progress monitor (Sec. IV-A ), was applied to the real exterior camera unchanged from simulation. The live rule fires when max progress stays below τ = 0.45 \tau{=}0.45 by a mid-skill deadline. Exterior vision limits detection. Scored in-sample the monitor looks near-perfect, but that estimate is leaked (the head was fit on rollouts of the same objects it scores). When scoring a new episode with known objects and on unseen objects, the deployment’s AUROC falls to the range in Table VII : wide at n = 45 n{=}45 and not separable from chance, so we report weak transfer and make no significant-detection claim. The gap is observability, since with exterior vision alone a failed grasp or dropped object is often invisible, even if the place motion still completes on camera. sections.heading: VI Discussion
sections.text: One mechanism explains the results. Seam failure is an off-support state rather than a miscalibrated policy, so only restoring the state clears it. This is why searching harder (best-of- K K ), swapping the policy (Diffusion Policy), or planning (a world model) all leave the seam unmoved. The ablation says what to restore: articulation and objects are complementary, and any single-component fix reaches only 0.13 0.13 – 0.27 0.27 of the 0.52 0.52 oracle (Table II ). The open problem is restoration quality. Even where restoration applies it recovers only half the oracle gap (Table IV ), and the object restorer we tried does not yet transfer (Sec. V-D ). We hypothesize the limiting factor is re-entry timing (when to hand control back) rather than component coverage: the monitor can re-fire mid-restoration, and a fixed hand-back tolerance is a crude proxy for “restored enough to resume.” A learned re-entry value function, plus enabling restoration by skill type (Sec. V-D ), are the natural next steps.

sections.heading: VII Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: We diagnosed long-horizon seam collapse as Observation-Space Shift, localized it causally to displaced articulation and secondary objects whose effects interact, and showed, through controls that fail from the same states, that the test-time-compute, stronger-base-policy, and world-model interventions we tested do not recover the seam, whereas restoration does. Our fully learned, non-privileged detect–restore–resume system improves full-chain success 3.5 × 3.5\times over the frozen base ( p = 0.047 p{=}0.047 ), reaching 51 % 51\% of a privileged oracle from cameras and proprioception alone. Limitations and future work. Our quantitative core is in simulation. On hardware the exterior-camera monitor is limited by observability, since a failed grasp is invisible without wrist and gripper sensing, the clearest next step. Restoration is defined only for drawer seams, so chains whose second seam displaces a free object stay unrecovered and need an object-restoration skill. Results use a single base-policy seed and an uncorrected n = 10 n{=}10 test, and the absolute L 2 L_{2} ( 0.265 0.265 ) is modest. Scaling seam data 10 × 10\times within the same distribution does not help ( 0.117 0.117 ). Whether broader training distribution randomization would is untested.

Although individual skills can be reliable in isolation, long-horizon task performance can degrade sharply when these skills are chained: each downstream skill must start from the state produced by its predecessor rather than from its training distribution. We study this failure mode, known as Observation-Space Shift (OSS), and investigate what aspects are responsible for such skill-seam failures. Through privileged simulator resets, we identify that the dominant shift arises from displaced scene state (e.g., an open drawer or secondary objects left behind by preceding skills), rather than from the robot joint configuration or the object manipulated by the downstream skill. To test this diagnosis, we build a fully learned detect–restore–resume system that restores the components the analysis identifies: a task-progress monitor detects the stall, a learned policy restores those components, and seam-robust fine-tuning lets the skill resume . It recovers the seam where every tested alternative fails, which is evidence for the diagnosis rather than a general purpose method. On the BOSS-44 benchmark, our system improves full-chain success from 7.6% to 26.5%, a 3.5 × 3.5\times improvement over the base policy and 51% of a privileged restoration oracle. In contrast, best-of- K K resampling, a Diffusion Policy, and world-model-based baselines fail to recover from the evaluated OSS seam states. During real-robot experiments on a real Franka arm running π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy, the same progress monitor is limited by external camera observability, yet closing the loop still recovers some otherwise-terminal failures. This motivates wrist and gripper sensing. These results suggest that some long-horizon composition failures are better addressed by restoring the scene before resuming the policy, rather than retrying from an off-support state. I Introduction Long-horizon robotic manipulation often requires composing multiple skills into a single task [ 1 , 2 ] . For example, a robot may first open a drawer, then move an object, and finally place it at a target location. A common strategy is to train individual manipulation skills independently and execute them sequentially in a chain at deployment. Although these skills can be reliable when evaluated from their own training distributions, long-horizon task performance can degrade drastically once they are chained together. The challenge arises at the skill seams , where one skill terminates and the next begins: A downstream skill does not start from the canonical initial states on which it was trained; instead, it inherits whatever scene state its predecessor leaves behind. For example, an “open drawer” skill may leave the drawer open before a “place bowl” skill, trained with the drawer closed, begins execution. The downstream skill is therefore asked to act from an unfamiliar state and may stall even though it succeeds reliably in isolation. This mismatch between the downstream skill’s training distribution and the state encountered during skill composition is known as Observation-Space Shift (OSS) [ 2 ] . On the three-skill chains studied in BOSS-44 [ 2 ] , success through the chain drops from 88.5 % 88.5\% after executing the first skill, to 34.3 % 34.3\% after two skills (one seam), and to 7.6 % 7.6\% after all three skills (two seams), despite the component skills achieving 79.0 % 79.0\% average success when evaluated independently from their canonical initial states. Fig. 1: Detect, restore, resume at a skill seam. A chained skill collapses when it starts from the previous skill’s off-support terminal state; a task-progress monitor detects the stall, a learned restoration skill returns the displaced scene to support, and the chain resumes. What changes at a skill seam that causes the downstream skill to fail? We consider three potential sources of shift: the preceding skill may (1) leave the robot arm in an unfamiliar state; (2) displace the object manipulated by the downstream skill; or (3) alter other elements of the scene. To identify which components are responsible, we diagnose OSS through privileged simulator interventions. Using a teleportation oracle and component-wise resets, we selectively restore different state components to their canonical values. We find that (1) resetting the robot arm provides little improvement; (2) the object manipulated by the downstream skill is typically already close to its canonical position; and (3) the dominant recovery comes from restoring articulated scene state (e.g., an open drawer) and secondary objects (i.e., other objects displaced by preceding skills but not manipulated by the downstream skill). Moreover, these effects are complementary: restoring articulation or secondary objects individually yields only partial gains, whereas restoring them jointly recovers substantially more of the oracle performance. This diagnosis suggests that recovery should modify the state responsible for the failure rather than repeatedly invoke the policy from off-support states. As shown in Fig. 1 , we introduce a detect–restore–resume framework: a fully learned, non-privileged system that recovers much of the oracle from cameras and proprioception alone. A task-progress monitor detects when execution has stalled. A learned restoration policy modifies the displaced scene state, after which the downstream skill resumes execution. Since learned restoration only approximately returns the scene to its canonical state, we additionally apply seam-robust prevention fine-tuning on post-restoration hand-off states to improve robustness during re-entry. On BOSS-44, our system improves three-skill full-chain success from 7.6 % 7.6\% to 26.5 % 26.5\% , compared with 51.8 % 51.8\% under a privileged oracle that exactly restores the scene to its canonical state. A matched re-home-and-retry baseline reaches only 12.9 % 12.9\% , showing that the improvement cannot be explained simply by additional execution attempts. Best-of- K K resampling and a Diffusion Policy trained on the same canonical demonstrations also fail from the evaluated OSS seam states, indicating that retrying or changing the policy architecture alone does not resolve these failures. On a real Franka arm with a π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy, the same monitor runs unchanged but transfers only weakly from an exterior camera. Closing the loop also recovers some otherwise-terminal failures, a proof of concept that isolates the observability (wrist and gripper sensing) as an important requirement for deployment. Our contributions are three-fold. • We provide a diagnosis of OSS at long-horizon skill seams. Through privileged simulator interventions, we show that skill-seam failures are driven primarily by displaced articulation and secondary scene objects. • We propose a learned detect–restore–resume framework for long-horizon skill composition. The system detects stalled execution, restores the displaced scene toward the downstream support, and resumes execution using only deployable observations at test time. • Experiments on both BOSS-44 demonstrate that our framework achieves a 3.5 × 3.5\times improvement in full-chain success, outperforming other baselines. We provide empirical analysis of when restoration is a better intervention than retry. On a real Franka, the same monitor runs unchanged but it limited by exterior-camera observability. Closing the loop recovers a fraction of otherwise-terminal failures, a proof of concept that motivates wrist and gripper sensing. II Related Work Skill chaining, observation-space shift, and recovery. Composing pretrained skills into long-horizon behavior is central to hierarchical and library-based control [ 3 , 4 , 2 , 1 ] , where a transition succeeds only when one skill’s termination region meets the next’s initiation set [ 5 , 6 ] . A seam is a violation of that condition. The mechanism is the behavior-cloning covariate shift at composition, where a downstream skill inherits a state its predecessor produced but never trained on [ 7 , 8 ] . This is not specific to small policies: generalist vision-language-action models [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] and modern imitation learners [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] clone actions and inherit the same off-support behavior when chained. Unlike work that reports chaining loss as an aggregate drop, we localize the shift causally to specific state components. Prior fixes act at training time, regularizing a skill’s terminal distribution toward the next initiation set [ 17 ] or appending recovery and correction data [ 18 ] . Test-time recovery instead retrieves and replays demonstration sub-trajectories [ 19 ] , backtracks to a prior skill, takes object-centric keypoint steps back onto the manifold [ 20 ] , or learns local RL recovery policies [ 21 ] . We test faithful instances of retrieval, backtracking, and library-inverse correction and find none re-manipulates the displaced scene. Our restoration skill supplies that behavior as a learned reset controller, the objective of reset-free RL and learned resets [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] , but invoked at a detected seam rather than every episode. It is trained with SAC [ 25 ] and RLPD [ 26 ] from real failure states and distilled to a camera-only student. We compare it against a training-time prevention condition built with data generation [ 27 ] rather than only asserting the distinction. Detection and test-time alternatives. Detecting task failure without labels has converged on task-progress and value estimation from pixels: Generative Value Learning [ 28 ] elicits per-frame completion from a VLM, and process-reward models such as Robometer [ 29 ] train per-frame progress on robot data. Our monitor keeps the progress-as-normalized-time target but trains a ∼ 1 \sim\!1 M-parameter head over a frozen encoder with an added success/stall contrast loss, and fires a calibrated stagnation trigger in the spirit of distribution-free failure detection [ 30 , 31 ] . Unlike runtime monitors that add temporal-consistency terms [ 32 ] or world-model prediction surprise, we find progress alone is the correctly signed signal at stalls. The alternative to restoration is planning or search: imagine-score-execute pipelines plan with learned dynamics [ 33 , 34 , 35 , 36 ] and sampling-based shooting (e.g., MPPI [ 37 ] ) selects actions by simulated return, while a separate line scales test-time compute by sampling K K rollouts and keeping the best [ 38 ] . Evaluated from OSS seams, a world model as generator, monitor, or planner gives no benefit or is falsified, and best-of- K K cannot select what the policy cannot produce. IV-A Detect: a task-progress monitor with a calibrated trigger Detect answers one question: has the current skill stopped making progress? A task-progress head scores each frame’s position within a skill, and the trigger fires when that score stops rising (Fig. 3 ). Prediction-surprise signals fail here: at seams the robot stalls, so the next frame is nearly identical and trivially predictable, and surprise becomes anti-predictive ((Sec. V-B )). A stalled robot cannot manufacture progress, so the progress signal stays correctly signed. Trigger. The alarm is progress-slope stagnation over an 8 8 -sample window (not absolute level, which is low early in every skill), fired when the statistic exceeds a threshold τ \tau for 3 3 consecutive samples. τ \tau is set by split-conformal calibration on success demos [ 30 ] . Since seam states are off-support its formal guarantee need not hold, so we fix the operating point empirically on cached rollouts ( 0.95 0.95 true-positive, 7 % 7\% false-alarm; Sec. V-E ). VI Discussion One mechanism explains the results. Seam failure is an off-support state rather than a miscalibrated policy, so only restoring the state clears it. This is why searching harder (best-of- K K ), swapping the policy (Diffusion Policy), or planning (a world model) all leave the seam unmoved. The ablation says what to restore: articulation and objects are complementary, and any single-component fix reaches only 0.13 0.13 – 0.27 0.27 of the 0.52 0.52 oracle (Table II ). The open problem is restoration quality. Even where restoration applies it recovers only half the oracle gap (Table IV ), and the object restorer we tried does not yet transfer (Sec. V-D ). We hypothesize the limiting factor is re-entry timing (when to hand control back) rather than component coverage: the monitor can re-fire mid-restoration, and a fixed hand-back tolerance is a crude proxy for “restored enough to resume.” A learned re-entry value function, plus enabling restoration by skill type (Sec.
